---------- Original Message ---------- 
From: Roger Mundry <roger_...@eva.mpg.de> 
Date: October 28, 2014 at 5:21 PM 
Subject: lme4: huge problem with model comparisons 

Dear all, 

my apologies for the mass mailing. If you are not using R (namely 
functions provided by the package lme4) you can safely remove this 
email, otherwise please read it carefully (it is important). 

I just stumbled across a huge problem that can happen in the context of 
model comparisons (e.g., full vs. null model) when each of the following 
three conditions are fulfilled: 
* the models were fitted using the function glmer or lmer; 
* there are missing data in the variables involved in the models; 
* the comparison is based on the R-function anova. 
What could happen in such a situation is that the two data sets on which 
the two models are based are no more the same since g/lmer (as other 
functions such as glm, lm, etc.) removes rows with missing values from 
the data before fitting the model. The big problem arises because for 
some reason the function anova still spits out the likelihood ratio 
test, even though this is completely invalid when the two data sets were 
not absolutely identical wrt the response (I pasted an example below 
demonstrating that). More specifically, since the simpler of the two 
models involves less variables it will likely be based on more data and 
this invariably makes the comparison anti-conservative (increased 
probability of significance in case the null-hypothesis is true). (my 
intuition tells me that the same applies when using the function drop1.) 

For you this means that you have to make sure that the two models to be 
compared are fitted on the exact same data. Below I show an example for 
how this can be achieved. Please don't hesitate to contact me in case 
you have further questions (but please don't do this by email but 
approach me in person). 

Again my apologies for the mass mail, but I felt this to be important 
and urgent. Have a nice evening, 

Roger 

here is some code demonstrating the problem and a solution: 
library(lme4)#load library 
#create data: 
xfac=as.factor(sample(letters[1:10], 100, replace=T))#random effect 
xcov=runif(100)#fixed effect 
xcov[sample(1:100, 10)]=NA#get some NAs into the fixed effect 
resp=rnorm(100)#response 
full=lmer(resp~xcov+(1|xfac), REML=F)#run full model 
null=lmer(resp~1+(1|xfac), REML=F)#run null model 
c(length(residuals(full)), length(residuals(null)))#the number data 
points use for the two models is different 
anova(null, full, test="Chisq")#compare the two models using anova 
#(note that this is highly significant although there is no influence of 
the covariate on the response) 

#how the can be solved: 
#step 1: get all variables needed (but only these) into one data frame 
test.data=data.frame(xfac, xcov, resp) 
#step 2: omit rows with NAs included (the function na.omit is what is 
really needed here; the other two are cosmetic) 
test.data=droplevels(data.frame(na.omit(test.data))) 
#run the models and the model comparison again: 
full=lmer(resp~xcov+(1|xfac), data=test.data, REML=F)#run full model 
null=lmer(resp~1+(1|xfac), data=test.data, REML=F)#run null model 
c(length(residuals(full)), length(residuals(null)))#the number data 
points use for the two models is the same now 
anova(null, full, test="Chisq")#compare the two models using anova 
#(note that it is (usually) not all significant anymore 

#the following lines show that for models run using the function glm 
this problem doesn't exist: 
xcov=runif(100) 
xcov[sample(1:100, 10)]=NA 
resp=exp(rnorm(100)) 
resp=rbinom(n=100, size=1, prob=resp/(1+resp)) 
full=glm(resp~xcov, family=binomial) 
null=glm(resp~1, family=binomial) 
c(length(residuals(full)), length(residuals(null))) 
anova(null, full, test="Chisq")
